blocks.text: We hope we shall do our readers a welcome service if, to what Bochart has so far adduced from the Arabs on the lizard ضب [ḍabb], we add what experts in these matters among our own writers report about it. Among these let the first be LEO AFRICANUS, who in Descript. Africae book 9, ch. 52, p. [?], Zurich ed. 1559, has this: The Dub (otherwise Dab) is an animal living in the deserts; in form it resembles the stellio, though it is somewhat thicker; in length it fills a forearm, in breadth four fingers. It does not drink water, and if anyone pours water on them, it dies on the spot. It hatches eggs in the manner of the tortoise, and it lacks venom. They are caught by the Arabs in the deserts; indeed I myself cut the throat of one I had caught, yet it gives out little blood. It is eaten roasted, with the skin removed, and has the flavour and taste of a small frog. In speed it resembles the lizard, and if during the hunt it is driven into an underground hole, with its tail remaining outside, it cannot be pulled out by any force; but when the opening has been widened with mattocks, it is taken by the hunters. When, three days after being killed, it is put on the fire, it moves no differently than if it had been freshly killed. But far more accurately HASSELQUIST described this animal in his Itiner. p. 353, German trans., under the name Lacerta Aegyptia cauda verticillata squamis denticulatis, pedibus pentadactylis [Egyptian lizard with whorled tail, denticulate scales, five-toed feet]. — Head roughly triangular, elongated, continuous with the neck and a little higher than it. — Snout blunt, very short, scarcely distinguishable from the head, flattened above, uneven, ending behind at the sides in two prominences, one on each side. — Eyes behind the snout, at the sides of the head, nearer the upper part of the head than the throat. Pupil black. Iris dark. Two small pits, one on each side, oblong, immediately above the eyes, behind the prominences of the snout. The area of the eyes deeper [relative to the prominences of the head and snout], oblong, sprinkled with very small tubercles. The space between the eyes oblong, slightly raised, slightly narrowed. [II, 473] Crown in the middle of the head, behind the said space, a little higher than it, transversely oblong, very short. The space behind the crown [the base of the head] slightly sloping, rather broad towards the rear, flat. Two small pits, oblong, rather broad, one on each side of this space, set obliquely. The sides of the head protuberant, uneven. — Two hollows, one on each side, behind these protuberances, at the base of the sides of the head, crescent-shaped, fairly deep, smooth, even, with a membranous floor; ears? — Nostrils 2, one on each side, fairly large, round, surrounded by a membranous margin, near the tip of the snout, immediately above the upper jaw. — Jaws equal, rather broad. Lips mobile, covering the jaws; the upper one ends on each side at the edges in scaly tubercles, which surround its margin and imitate small teeth. Each jaw is composed of bones. These tubercles number 12 on each side, of which the 4 rear ones are pointed, the rest convex and very blunt. The tip of this lip smooth. The lower lip is covered at its margin with simple, oblong scales. — The small teeth are serrations of the jawbones; in the upper jaw about 43: three in front, and 20 at the sides on each side; of the front ones the middle is the broadest, slightly convex, with a semicircular margin, longer than all the others. The other two slightly pointed, slightly convex, shorter than the middle one, one on each side of it, set against its side. The front lateral ones, 8, very minute, close together, with a nearly linear tip; the rear ones, 12, larger, with distinct tips, somewhat pointed, the last ones blunter. Small teeth in the lower jaw about 20 on each side. The front ones very short, scarcely distinguishable; the rest very blunt, close together, longer. — Neck cylindrical, continuous with the head, of its thickness and twice as long, rather broad at the base. — Body strongly flattened on both sides, narrowed towards each end, more so behind but over a shorter space; less in front, but over a somewhat longer space; broad in the middle. — Sides convex, slightly protuberant, bellied. — Tail cylindrical, continuous with the body and of the same length, elongated, gradually narrower up to the tip, covered above with spiny scales arranged vertically, but below with oblong, smooth scales. The rings of scales are 22, the larger composed of about 10 scales, and successively of fewer. Each scale oblong, forming a parallelogram with truncated corners, ending behind in a spine which projects at an obtuse angle from the body of the scale. — Feet 4, two at each end of the body. The front ones immediately below the neck, at the sides of the body, cylindrical, shorter than the hind ones by about half; thighs short, not thicker than the shanks; shanks twice as long as the thighs, continuous with them and distinguished from them only by the joint. The hind ones immediately above the tail, at the sides of the head, almost twice as long as the front ones. Thighs as long as the shanks, much thicker than them, slightly narrower below. Shanks slightly compressed in the lower half, cylindrical in the upper. Toes of each foot 5, a little smaller on the front feet, on all compressed, scaly, unequal; the two outer ones shorter than the rest, equal; of the rest, the one next to the inner is a little longer than it, the one following it longer, and the one after that, the fourth from the inner, the longest of all. Lobes of the feet several. Claws end all the toes, compressed, sloping, pointed, slightly hooked. [II, 474] — Scales cover the head, feet and whole body: on the head hexagonal and octagonal, mixed, large, raised, smooth; on the feet rhomboidal and roundish, the front ones flat, smooth; the hind ones in some cases furnished with a pointed spine rising from their middle; on the toes oblong, convex, blunt at the tip, imbricate, arranged in three lines on each toe. Scales of the back slightly imbricate, very minute, roundish. A line runs through the middle of the whole back, composed of indistinct scales, yet perceptible to the eye. Scales of the abdomen four-sided, imbricate, smooth, three times as long as the dorsal ones, more raised. — Tubercles, scaly, fragile, raised, roundish, are seen 1) scattered here and there over the upper part of the head and neck; 2) over the sides of the head, especially towards the tail, where some are irregularly scattered. 3) A line of these tubercles runs underneath along the middle of the thighs; these are a little larger, whitish, marked with a dark dot in the middle. — Cuticle thin, easily stripped off. — Colour: head, back and feet dark. Abdomen, toes and tail whitish-brown. Throat variegated with dark and yellowish. — Total length from the tip of the snout to the tip of the tail 3¼ spans. Of the head with snout 2 inches. Of the neck 3 inches. Of the body 1 span 2 inches. Of the tail 1 span 2 inches. — Breadth of the head above the crown and of the neck 1½ inches. Of the body near the neck 1 palm, near the tail 2 inches. Of the body near the middle 1½ palms. — Height of the front foot 1 palm 1 inch, of the hind 2 palms. Thickness of the neck and head 5 inches. Of the snout 3 inches. Of the tail at the base 5 inches, near the middle 4 inches, towards the end 1 inch. At the tip of the smallest toe. Of the front shanks and thighs 3 inches, of the hind thighs 4½ inches. Of the hind shanks 3 inches. — Breadth of the lobes of the foot 1 inch. — Length of the smallest toe 2½ inches. — Habitat: Egypt, plain and mountainous. So far Hasselquist. To be added is FORSKAL in Descriptt. Animall. p. 13: „Lacerta Aegyptia. To the Arabs Dabb. Thighs terete, without warts. Tail whorled, not long. Scales spreading, subconical, mucronate. Body naked, wrinkled.“
